'''''Iris domestica''''', commonly known as '''leopard lily''',<ref>{{Cite book|url=http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf|title=English Names for Korean Native Plants|publisher=[[Korea National Arboretum]]|year=2015|isbn=978-89-97450-98-5|location=Pocheon|pages=371|access-date=26 January 2017|via=[[Korea Forest Service]]|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170525105020/http://www.forest.go.kr/kna/special/download/English_Names_for_Korean_Native_Plants.pdf|archive-date=25 May 2017}}</ref> '''blackberry lily''', and '''leopard flower''', is an [[ornamental plant]] in the family [[Iridaceae]].<ref name="cabi">{{cite web |title=''Iris domestica'' (blackberry lily) |url=https://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/62815878 |publisher=CABI |access-date=17 December 2021 |date=22 November 2019}}</ref> In 2005, based on molecular DNA sequence evidence, ''Belamcanda chinensis'', the sole species in the genus ''Belamcanda'', was transferred to the genus ''Iris'' and renamed ''Iris domestica''.<ref>Goldblatt P, Mabberley DJ (2005) ''Belamcanda'' Included in ''Iris'', and the New Combination ''I. domestica'' (Iridaceae: Irideae). Novon: A Journal for Botanical Nomenclature: Vol. 15, No. 1 pp. 128–132</ref>

==Description==
A [[perennial herb]], ''I. domestica'' may grow to a height of {{convert|0.6|-|1|m}}, with its [[rhizome]]s in shallow ground, extending horizontally.<ref name=cabi/> It has 3-5-stems and 8–14 leaves per stem growing in a [[hand fan|fan]], with flowers ascending proximally having orange-red scattered spots of darker pigment, blooming during summer.<ref name=cabi/> The seed pods open in the fall, showing clusters of black, shiny seeds whose resemblance to those of a [[blackberry]] gives the plant its common name, "blackberry lily".<ref name=cabi/> The plant is hardy to [[USDA plant hardiness zone]] 5 and is propagated by seeds or division.

In the wild, it grows in [[grassland]]s, pastures, forest clearings, [[meadow]]s, and mountainous regions or shrublands.<ref name=cabi/> Although it has escaped cultivation in many regions, it is not considered to have potential as an [[invasive species]].<ref name=cabi/>

==Synonyms==
Its synonyms are ''Epidendrum domesticum'' [[Carolus Linnaeus|L.]], ''Vanilla domestica'' ([[Carolus Linnaeus|L.]]) [[George Claridge Druce|Druce]], ''Belamcanda punctata'' [[Conrad Moench|Moench]], ''Gemmingia chinensis'' ([[Carolus Linnaeus|L.]]) [[Otto Kuntze|Kuntze]], ''Ixia chinensis'' [[Carolus Linnaeus|L.]], ''Morea chinensis'', and ''Pardanthus chinensis'' [[John Bellenden Ker Gawler|Ker Gawl.]])

==Distribution==
The plant is native to Eastern Asia and has been cultivated worldwide in [[subtropical]] and [[temperate climate]]s.<ref name=cabi/><ref name="kew">{{cite web |title=''Iris domestica'' |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:60438342-2 |publisher=Plants of the World Online, Kew Royal Botanic Gardens |access-date=17 December 2021 |date=2017}}</ref> Due to the ornamental value of its attractive flowers, the plant was distributed to Europe as early as the 18th century and the United States and [[Caribbean|Caribbean countries]] in the 19th century.<ref name=cabi/>

==Uses==
''I. domestica'' is a common ornamental plant in private and public gardens, [[zoo]]s, and floral displays.<ref name=cabi/> Its flowers provide [[nectar]] and [[pollen]] to insects and birds.<ref name=cabi/> The plant has been used in [[traditional medicine]].<ref name=cabi/>
